extracted.intended_audience: readers of colonial-era ethnography; colonial administrators and missionaries
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-length ethnographic description of West African funeral, spirit, inheritance, and customary-legal practices, reporting tribal-specific rules, rituals, and rationales. Useful for understanding native social-legal standards and ceremonial requirements around death and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Killing of twins and associated mother-killings
rubrics_metrics.description: A widely diffused custom in parts of the Niger Delta where twins (and sometimes the mother) are killed; relatives of the sufferer may also be killed on suspicion of witchcraft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes the custom causes ‘pitiful waste of life’ and may provoke further killings; local explanations are often given as 'It was the custom of our fathers.' The underlying idea is obscure and resistant to outsider inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calabar practice: burying the dead under the house and separate head-burial for chiefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Calabar people bury beneath the house; for a great chief the head is cut off and buried in secrecy elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Body is buried a few days after death but the spirit-burial is the truly important part; secrecy around chiefs' head-burials is customary for reasons given elsewhere in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate spirit-burial (soul-burial) delayed until resources available
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit (soul) is regarded as malevolent and must be buried/made appropriately; families save wealth to perform a separate spirit-burial, which may occur a year or more after body-burial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because spirit-burial is expensive, there is often a long interval; mourners remain in a state (e.g., unwashed) until the spirit is properly buried. This delay structures mourning duration and widow confinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body-drying and temporary storage (Cabinda/Loango)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Cabinda and Loango, the body is placed on a wooden platform and dried with slow fires and a mat roof until it can be wrapped and kept in a coffin until funds allow final burial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative to immediate burial; practical measure to preserve the corpse while awaiting resources for the full funeral/ soul-burial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dualla death-dances scheduled on 3rd, 7th, and 9th days
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the Duallas death-dances must be celebrated on the third, seventh, and ninth day after death because the spirit is particularly present then.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These fixed-day ceremonies reflect beliefs about when the spirit remains at home; delay in making the 'devil' causes the spirit to become fractious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destruction of bodies believed to contain dangerous or wanderer-souls
rubrics_metrics.description: For bodies thought to house dangerous souls or 'wanderer-souls' (souls that repeatedly inhabit infants), the body may be destroyed—beaten to pulp, cut up, limbs broken, or scattered—to prevent the soul returning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices vary from breaking a leg (as warning to a returning soul) to cutting the corpse into small pieces and scattering them: intended to prevent reincarnation in the family and stop recurring infant deaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ncomi as funeral specialists and non-burial coffins
rubrics_metrics.description: Ncomi (Fernan Vaz tribe) are called in as specialists to conduct complex death-dances; they place bodies in coffins (barrels, gun-cases, trade boxes) which are not buried but deposited in special forest places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ncomi’s ritual performance may be lengthy and structured; the text recounts social dynamics (audience boredom, expectations) and the practice of keeping coffins in forest repositories rather than burying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forest heaps/mounds (Abe) as burying grounds of the Ajumbas
rubrics_metrics.description: Along some rivers are stretches of bush containing many heaps of branches and leaves; underneath each heap are remains—these are used as burying grounds (Abe) of the Ajumbas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are not mould-covered mounds but heaps of branches; such sites appear as uninhabited stretches of bush to outsiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Widows and certain accused persons remain unwashed and confined until soul-burial
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who escape execution on witchcraft charges (widows, relatives) must remain in a state of filth and abasement, not removing vermin, confined to their huts until the soul-burial is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is to avoid damaging the dead man's soul; widows also lose practical legal rights (e.g., over property) during this period and bear heavy funeral-related expenses including hosting visitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mourning practices: hair cutting, unwashed state, and duration linked to soul-burial
rubrics_metrics.description: All mourners typically remain unwashed; mourning includes various hair-cutting styles (shave all, none, half, etc.). The mourning period commonly equals the interval between death and the soul-burial (or devil-making).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific tribal durations vary; e.g., among the Ewe of Togoland the widow stays in the hut 5–6 weeks and is monitored for six further months before remarriage is permitted. The widow must not remarry while the husband's soul is near.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Lifting' custom with soap gift (M'pongwe and Igalwa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mourners sit on the floor unwashed; a friend comes in to 'lift them up', bringing a small present often including a piece of soap—an act that aids the transition from enforced uncleanness to normal social condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This custom is surviving in modified form in urban areas (Libreville, Glass) where relatives no longer sit unwashed but the ceremonial 'lifting' persists symbolically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roadside bough shelters (spirit beds) with deceased's belongings
rubrics_metrics.description: Erected outside villages along roads are bough-platform shelters resembling beds where the deceased's bedding, pillows, household utensils, dolls etc. are laid for the spirit to rest while awaiting burial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items are often deliberately damaged before being laid; pillows are oriented so a lying person would look toward the village. Food and spirits are placed and offerings poured periodically. These are attended only while the spirit awaits burial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delta belief in rapid reincarnation and role of burial goods in determining reincarnation status
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Niger Delta souls are thought to return quickly to earth in new babies; the wealth sent down with a man indicates the class of baby the soul will be 'repacked' into—real estate (wives/slaves) matters for perceived status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this, sending only trade goods (cloth, oil) is not felt equivalent to sending wives/slaves; relatives fear misrepresenting a chief's status and the risk of his return as a slave if insufficient 'real estate' accompanies him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Killing at funerals as a deterrent against poisoning and as retinue for the dead
rubrics_metrics.description: Killing wives and slaves at funerals serves two perceived purposes: to provide a retinue/riches for the dead in the afterlife and to discourage poisoning (people restrained from murdering kinsmen if they risk losing slaves/wives at death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government efforts to prevent such killings can have unintended consequences by removing social deterrents, leading chiefs to complain about proliferation of witches and loss of deterrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: N'dok (Creek Town) cleansing ceremony using Nbakim images
rubrics_metrics.description: Nbakim—large grotesque wooden images with rags—are displayed, offerings placed, then carried in a noisy procession through the town and finally thrown into the river to clear wandering spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The procession's noise drives spirits into the images; throwing the images into the river destroys or sends the spirits elsewhere. New images are made afterward for future use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customary legal principle: 'they should take who have the power, and they should keep who can'
rubrics_metrics.description: Underlying African law is a practical principle that advantage accrues to those with power; this affects inheritance and property distribution, often disadvantaging women and children without powerful relatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite this, there exists among Negroes and Bantus a recognised code of law with avenues for appeal if one can marshal resources to use it; customs can often be traced to utilitarian or natural origins but some are fossilised by veneration of ancestors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance rules vary: brother-as-heir, chief-slave inheritance, or eldest/preferred-son
rubrics_metrics.description: Different tribes follow different inheritance rules: many prefer the brother by the same mother as heir; in some tribes the eldest/influential son succeeds; in others the chief slave may inherit; ju-ju sometimes specify passing to the son of the chief wife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These variations reflect aims like keeping the 'house' estate together and avoiding transfer into the hands of weak claimants (women, young children). Local marriage customs (e.g., purchase-based legal marriage in Cameroon) affect who is recognised as eligible heirs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palaver/tribal adjudication practices and peculiar pleas
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes (e.g., inheritance) are resolved via palaver where each side repeatedly states facts; unusual pleas (e.g., 'This man cannot inherit because his parents married for love') may be advanced but local legal norms (e.g., marriage by purchase) determine validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The palaver can be long and repetitive; success may depend on skill, patience, and influence, and European presence has altered some practices near trading stations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community voting for 'house' inheritance (Bonny River/Opobo)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Bonny River and Opobo the distribution of a house's property is settled primarily by a vote of the free men of the house; the chosen successor must then be ratified by other house chiefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: European (white trader) influence has altered these customs in port towns, complicating efforts to discern pure native forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customary trial evidence and punishments: theft, mortgage, torts, and ordeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons are tried for theft using circumstantial evidence, direct testimony, and ordeal. Mortgage laws resemble European ones; torts are generally not recognised. Punishments (e.g., for adultery) may be severe in theory (death) but are often commuted or handled via fines or substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example cases show practical adjudication (e.g., canoe loan damage leading to compensation). Ordeals and spiritual explanations coexist with commonsense factors (bribing witch-doctors, use of emetics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canoe-loan customary obligation (case example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When A lends his canoe to B, the implicit condition (common in African loans) is that it be returned in the same state as lent (allowing fair wear and tear); failure may lead to compensation even if damage occurred due to a third party or 'force majeure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrated case (A v. B v. C) demonstrates that local judges may enforce restitution to the original owner and that local defences (e.g., act of God, non-slave status of third party) may be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adultery laws and enforcement practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Adultery is theoretically punishable by death in many coastal societies, and chiefs sometimes impose severe punishments (including death by flogging); in practice penalties are frequently commuted to fines or by substitution of a sacrificial person (e.g., a slave) if the accused is wealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adultery accusations are socially dangerous and often used extortionately; chiefs commonly subject wives to ordeals, especially after major family ceremonies.
